newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers blast Social Security Web site privacy.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers blast Social Security Web site privacy.

text.p: Top lawmakers worried that the confidential financial records of millions of Americans had been put at risk asked the government on Wednesday to stop posting sensitive Social Security data on the Internet.

The Internet Web site recently launched by the Social Security Administration allows individuals to look up earnings and benefit estimate statements after entering a few key bits of personal information.

Republican and Democratic Senate leaders said in a letter they wanted the service halted until the SSA can convene an independent panel of computer and privacy experts to recommend additional safeguards to ensure confidentiality.

Republican Leader Trent Lott and Democratic Leader Tom Daschle signed the letter sponsored by Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth of Delaware and ranking Democrat Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York.

The SSA last month began offering the service to make it easier for people to access their financial records and plan for retirement. Using a name, Social Security number, mother's maiden name, birthdate and place of birth, an individual can look up decades of past earnings records and projected Social Security benefits.
Some privacy experts have said it may be too easy for scam artists or nosy friends and relatives to gain access to the confidential information.

The SSA said it was confident the data is secure but was reviewing the Web site at http://www.ssa.gov. In the past, people wanting such information had to go to a local Social Security office or write to the agency.
"We are monitoring and evaluating the use of the Web site and the security measures that are protecting it," SSA spokesman Rich Hensley said.
In the House, Pennsylvania Democratic Representative Paul Kanjorski said he would introduce a bill to bar the agency from posting earnings and benefit estimate statements on the Web site.

Kentucky Republican Representative Jim Bunning, chairman of the House Ways and Means subcommittee that oversees the SSA, wrote to the agency asking for a thorough review of the service. "While I appreciate SSA's desire to provide fast and expedient service, such action should not compromise the privacy of Americans," Bunning told the agency.

Hensley said the Web site had been getting about 3,000 queries a day since it was made available about a month ago. It got 85,000 on Tuesday, probably due in part to a spate of news reports about the site and possible privacy concerns.
In fact, some people who have tried to look at their records have been unable to gain access because so many people are trying to view the site.
